nameStory: Aizoon Stonecrop gets its name from two sources: 'aizoon' comes from the Greek words meaning 'always living,' referring to its hardy, drought-resistant nature. The 'stonecrop' part of the name comes from these plants' amazing ability to grow in rocky crevices and stone walls where most other plants would struggle to survive.
description: Aizoon Stonecrop is a low-growing succulent plant with thick, fleshy leaves that help it store water like a tiny cactus. This hardy perennial typically grows 6-12 inches tall and spreads to form dense mats of blue-green foliage. In summer, it produces clusters of bright yellow star-shaped flowers that attract bees and butterflies. Originally from Asia, it's now grown as an ornamental plant in gardens and can occasionally escape cultivation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, succulent leaves that feel rubbery and cool to the touch, arranged alternately along the stems with distinctly toothed edges that look like tiny saw teeth

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow star-shaped flowers with 5 pointed petals, clustered together in dense, flat-topped groups that smell faintly sweet

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with stems that root where they touch soil, creating carpet-like colonies

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy reddish-brown stems that feel firm and slightly waxy, often with a purplish tinge in full sun

habitat: In New England, Aizoon Stonecrop is extremely rare, with only one recorded observation, likely from a garden escape or planted specimen. When found, it would typically be in rocky, well-drained areas like stone walls, rocky slopes, or abandoned garden sites where it can tolerate poor, dry soil.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of thick, blue-green leaves. Plants begin spreading and filling out their mat-like form.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering season with bright yellow star-shaped blooms covering the plant from June through August. Leaves are at their thickest and most succulent.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may take on reddish or purplish tints. Seeds develop and disperse, though plants mainly spread by rooting stems.
seasonality.winter: In milder areas, leaves persist and turn more reddish-purple. In harsh New England winters, above-ground parts may die back but roots survive to regrow in spring.

funFact: This little succulent is actually edible and is used in traditional Asian cuisine, where the young leaves are added to soups and salads for their crisp, slightly sour taste - like nature's own sour candy!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other stonecrops, but Aizoon Stonecrop's distinctly toothed leaf edges set it apart from most relatives which have smooth-edged leaves. Remember: 'Aizoon has teeth' - those little saw-tooth leaf margins are your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'stonecrop,' this plant was recently moved from the familiar Sedum genus to the newer Phedimus genus based on genetic studies. You may still see it sold in nurseries under its old name Sedum aizoon, which can cause confusion for plant enthusiasts trying to identify it.
compareHints: Aizoon Stonecrop differs from its Phedimus relatives by having the most prominently toothed leaf margins - those little saw teeth are much more pronounced than in Caucasian Stonecrop or Kamchatka Stonecrop. It also tends to have a more upright growth habit compared to the very low, creeping forms of most other species in this genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its stonecrop relatives, Caucasian stonecrop is distinguished by its opposite leaf arrangement and two-ranked growth pattern (leaves in two rows).
Among its Phedimus relatives in New England, yellow stonecrop is distinguished by its compact, mounded growth habit and consistently bright yellow spring flowers.
Hybrid Stonecrop has noticeably larger, more paddle-shaped leaves than its relatives like Caucasian Stonecrop, which has smaller, more rounded leaves.

Among its Phedimus relatives in New England, Kamchatka Stonecrop stands out for its distinctly orange-tinted flowers - Caucasian Stonecrop has purer yellow or pinkish blooms, while other related species tend toward bright yellow or white.
